runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text: A downstroke drags your pick or fingers from the low (thick) strings toward the high (thin) strings, usually giving a fuller, punchier sound since you catch more strings. An upstroke goes the opposite way, high to low, and tends to sound lighter and thinner since you often only catch the top few strings — it's what gives strumming patterns their bounce and momentum between the downs.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?

An upstroke moves the opposite way, from high strings toward the low ones, and is generally lighter/quieter, used to fill in the off-beats. runs.text: A down strum drags your pick (or fingers) downward across the strings toward the floor, usually hitting the lower-to-higher pitched strings in sequence — it's the strong, natural stroke that falls on the beat. An up strum reverses that, moving upward, catching fewer strings (often just the top 3-4) and sounding lighter/thinner — it's used on the off-beats to keep the rhythm moving without over-accenting. Alternating D and U is what gives strumming patterns their groove instead of sounding like a flat series of hits.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text:
A down strum sweeps your pick (or thumb) from the low strings toward the high ones — think bass to treble. An up strum goes the opposite way, from high strings back down toward the lows.

Down strokes naturally land on the beats and sound strong and full; up strokes usually sit on the "and" between beats and sound lighter, which is what gives strumming its groove — think **D DU UD**: the downs carry the pulse, the ups keep the motion flowing.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text: A downstroke sweeps the pick (or your fingers) from the low strings toward the high strings — toward the floor, so it sounds the bass notes first. An upstroke goes the other way, from the high strings back toward the low. Because the strings get hit in opposite order, on the upstroke the higher, thinner strings tend to ring out more, so it naturally sounds a bit lighter and works well on the off-beats between downstrokes.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text:
A down strum sweeps the pick (or thumb) from the lowest strings toward the floor, hitting the bass strings first; an up strum sweeps back from the high e toward the low strings. In the app, a downstroke is written **D** and an upstroke **U**.

The practical difference is feel: downstrokes land on the beat and sound fuller and more grounded, while upstrokes naturally fall on the "and" between beats and feel lighter — think of the classic "down, down-up, up-down-up."

runs.text:
In Travis picking, the assignment is classic thumb–and–fingers:

- **Thumb (p)** alternates the bass on the low strings — usually the root on the 6th or 5th string and the fifth on the 4th (or 5th), so the thumb "walks" between two bass notes.
- **Index (i)** plays the 3rd string (G).
- **Middle (m)** plays the 2nd string (B).
- **Ring (a)** plays the 1st string (high e).

So the steady pattern often falls as: thumb, index, thumb, middle (and add ring for a fuller arpeggio). Keep the thumb moving on a steady beat and let the fingers pick the upper strings gently — that steady bass is what gives Travis picking its feel.

runs.input: how do I read tab?
runs.text: Tab reads like this: the six lines are your strings, with the highest-pitched string (high e) on top and the lowest (low E) on the bottom. Each number tells you which fret to press on that string, and you read left to right in time — the dashes are beats you let ring or rest. So a "3" on the top line means press the 3rd fret of the high e string; a "0" means play that string open. Numbers stacked vertically are played together as a chord. Want me to make a simple pattern so you can see how it sounds?

runs.input: how do I read tab?
runs.text:
Reading tab is pretty simple once you know the two rules. The six lines are your strings, and the top line is the thinnest string (high e), the bottom line is the thickest (low E) — so it's drawn as if the neck is lying in front of you, headstock to your left.

Numbers tell you which fret to press on that string: a `0` means play the string open, a `2` on the A line means fret the A string at the 2nd fret. Dashes just mark time — they mean "keep the string ringing" or "rest" depending on context, while the string letter stays the same. When numbers are stacked vertically, you play them together as a chord; when they appear one after another left to right, you play them in sequence.

If you want to practice, I can turn any chord progression into a beginner tab pattern so you can see how numbers sit on the lines — just tell me the chords and the feel you want.

runs.input: how do I read tab?
runs.text: You read tab as six lines, one per string, with the high e on top and the low E on the bottom. The numbers tell you which fret to press on that string — a 0 is an open string, and "x" (or nothing played) means that string isn't struck. Read left to right in time: each dash or position is one beat subdivision, so notes stacked vertically are played together as a chord, and notes in sequence are picked one after another. The vertical lines (|) mark the end of each bar.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text:
A down strum drags the pick or your nails from the low strings toward the high ones; an up strum comes back the other way, from high to low. Because of that, the down is naturally heavier and lands on the beat, while the up is lighter and usually fills the "and" between beats — it's also why patterns like D DU UD feel like they swing.

Try it slowly on one chord and listen to the low string ring on the downs and the high strings catch on the ups; it'll make the feel obvious.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text:
A down strum is the pick moving from the low strings toward the high strings (downward across the strings, the way you'd naturally flick your hand down). An up strum is the reverse — moving from the high strings back toward the low ones, on the way back up.

The main practical difference is sound and where it lands in the beat. Downs tend to be stronger and carry the accent, so they usually fall on the beat; ups are lighter and often sit on the offbeats (the "and" between beats), which is what gives patterns like D DU UD their bounce. Most players also angle the pick slightly so downs and ups glide through the strings at a similar volume — if your ups sound weak or snag, that's usually the fix.

runs.input: what's the difference between a down strum and an up strum?
runs.text:
A down strum is played with the back of your fingernails or the pick moving from the low strings toward the high strings — it lands on the beat, a little heavier, and it's the stroke that carries the pulse. An up strum moves from high strings back to low, usually on the offbeats ("and"), lighter and shorter, and it's what fills the space between the beats.

The pairing is the whole basis of strumming patterns: down strokes mark the beat, up strokes answer them. If you want to feel it, "D DU UD" is the classic — two down strokes then the up-down pair that gives it the lift.

runs.input: which fingers should play which strings in Travis picking?
runs.text:
Travis picking is thumb plus three fingers, and the assignment is fixed by string:

- **Thumb (p):** the three bass strings — 6, 5 and 4. It alternates between them, usually root on the beat and the fifth (or an octave) between.
- **Index (i):** string 3
- **Middle (m):** string 2
- **Ring (a):** string 1

So on a C chord the thumb goes 5–4–6–4 (or 5–3–6–3 depending on the voicing), while i, m, a take 3, 2, 1 in any order you like against it. Keep the thumb steady and independent — that alternating bass is the whole point, and it should never stop while the fingers move.

runs.input: how do I read tab?
runs.text:
Tab is six lines, one per string, with the highest string on top:

```
e|--0--1--3--|
B|--1--------|
G|--0--------|
D|-----------|
A|--3--------|
E|-----------|
```

The numbers are frets, not fingers — 0 means play the string open, 3 means press the third fret. Reading left to right, the notes sound in the order they appear; numbers stacked in a column are played together as a chord. The vertical spacing tells you rhythm only roughly, so listen to the song for the timing, or use the app's own slots if you want it exact.

runs.input: how do I read tab?
runs.text:
Tab is just six lines, one per string, with the string numbers going from the thinnest at the top (1, high e) down to the thickest at the bottom (6, low E). Numbers on a line are the frets to press; read left to right, and notes stacked vertically are played together as a chord.

If the numbers sit in a row on one line it's a single-note line, and if they alternate between a low string and the higher ones it's usually a fingerpicking pattern — the low notes are the thumb taking the bass. Want me to make you a short pattern so you can see how it lines up?

runs.input: how do I read tab?
runs.text:
Reading tab is easier than it looks once you know the layout. Six lines = six strings, with the **high e on top** (string 1) and the **low E at the bottom** (string 6) — the same order you'd see if you laid the guitar on your lap facing you.

- **Numbers** are frets: 0 means open, 3 means press the 3rd fret. A number sits on the string you play.
- **Time flows left to right.** Numbers stacked vertically are played together; numbers spread out are played one after another.
- Common extras: h = hammer-on, p = pull-off, / and \ = slide up and down, x = muted/dead note, and a curved line or ~ = let it ring.

The trickiest habit to break is the string order — it's upside-down compared to looking down at your own guitar. If you want, I can make a simple pattern so you can see the strings and frets laid out in the app.
